title: An encapsulated bank account
instructions:
## Hide the balance behind methods

Write a class `BankAccount` whose balance can only change through its methods.

- `new BankAccount(owner, opening)` sets the owner and an opening balance (which must not be negative: throw an `Error`).
- `deposit(amount)` adds a positive amount; a zero or negative amount throws an `Error`.
- `withdraw(amount)` subtracts a positive amount but throws an `Error` with the message `Insufficient funds` when the balance would go below zero.
- `getBalance()` returns the balance; `getOwner()` returns the owner.
- Keep the balance in a `#balance` private field (or a closure) so `account.balance` is `undefined`.

The course uses Java; the class syntax, constructors, private fields and exceptions here map one to one.
hints: if (opening < 0) throw new Error("Opening balance cannot be negative");
withdraw: if (amount <= 0) throw ...; if (amount > this.#balance) throw new Error("Insufficient funds");
A # field is only visible inside the class, so a.balance is undefined from outside.

checks.label: Deposits and withdrawals change the balance through the methods
Overdrafts and bad amounts are refused
Uses a private field
checks.message: Declare #balance as a private field so it cannot be changed from outside.

realityNote: In Java the same class has a private double balance, a constructor, and throws IllegalArgumentException or a custom InsufficientFundsException; the principle, that invariants live inside the class, is the whole point of encapsulation.
